chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar, from Yunus, from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man happens to be in his house, then he is absent from it for thirty years, and he leaves his family in it. Then news of his death comes to us, and we do not know what occurred in his house, nor do we know what occurred for him in terms of children — we only know that we are not aware that he made any change in his house, nor that any child was born to him, and this house should not be divided among his heirs whom he left in the house until two just witnesses testify that this is the house of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, who died and left it as an inheritance between so-and-so and so-and-so. Should we testify to this?' He said: 'Yes.'

I said: 'A man has a slave and a slave-girl, and he says: "My slave has absconded and my slave-girl has absconded." They are found in the city, and the judge requires of him proof that this is the slave of so-and-so, who was neither sold nor gifted. Should we testify to this when we are required to do so, while we do not know if any change has occurred?' He said: 'Whenever the slave or slave-girl of a Muslim is absent from his hand, or is absent from you, do not testify about it.'

key_terms.أَبَقَ: Abaq — the flight/absconding of a slave, a recognized legal category in classical Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.الْبَيِّنَة: Bayyina — legal proof or evidence, typically two reliable witnesses
key_terms.الْمِيرَاث: Miras — inheritance, the division of a deceased person's estate according to Islamic law
key_terms.شَاهِدَا عَدْلٍ: Two witnesses of just character — the minimum standard for valid testimony in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: Can witnesses testify about property or slaves they have not seen recently according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Mu'awiya ibn Wahb asked Imam al-Sadiq (AS) two questions about the limits of permissible testimony: first, whether witnesses may testify about the inheritance of a man absent for thirty years, and second, whether witnesses may testify about ownership of runaway slaves. The Imam affirmed testimony in the first case (when witnesses can state facts they last knew to be true), but prohibited testimony in the second case — establishing the principle that witnesses may not testify about matters that have passed from their direct knowledge or observation. This reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that testimony (shahadah) must be grounded in direct, current knowledge, not mere prior assumption.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail Bin Marrar, from Yunus, from Muawiya Bin Wahab who said,

‘I said to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, ‘A man happened to be in his house, then he was absent from it for thirty years, and left his family in it. Then came to us (news of) his death, and we do not know what occurred in his house, nor do we know what occurred for him from the children except that we know that we do not know something was in his house nor some birth occurred for him, nor had this house been divided between his inheritors whom he had left in the house, until there testified two just witnesses that this is the house of so and so, son of so and so, who died and left it as an inheritance between so and so, and so and so. Should we testify upon this?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes’.

I said, ‘The man happened to have the slave and the slave girl for him. So he is saying, ‘My slave absconded, and my slave girl absconded’. So they were found in the city. So the judge assigned for it the production of the proof that this is a slave of so and so, not being sold nor being gifted. Should we testify upon this, when he assigns us and we do not know anything of the event?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘For everything which is absent from the hand of the Muslim person, his slave or slave girl, or absent from you, do not testify upon it’.
en.sarwar: 4. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ’Isma‘il ibn Marrar from Yunus from Mu‘awiyah ibn Wahab who has narrated the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who has a house and he remains absent from it for thirty years; but he leaves his family there, then news of his death comes. We do not know what may have happened in his house as well as to his children. We however, do not know of anything happening to his house and no birth of children has happened to him. This house is not divided among his heirs whom he had left in his house so that two just witnesses can testify that this house is the house of so and so son of so and so who has died and has left behind as legacy for so and so. Can we testify about it? He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, you can do so.’

I then said that a man has a slave and slave woman. He says that his slave has run away, his slave woman has run away and they are found in the town. The judge asks for proof that this is the slave of so and so whom he has not sold or gifted; if we can testify about it if we are asked and we do not know if anything has happened or not. He (the Imam) said, ‘Whatever goes out of the hands of a Muslim man, slave or slave woman or is absent from you, do not testify about it.’”
